lt:L1.01:0.text: Sam woke up to a loud bang. It was not thunder — it was the neighbor fixing his old truck again!

lt:L1.01:1.text: Sam's little sister covered her ears and laughed. "That truck is louder than a drum," she said.

lt:L1.01:2.text: Their mother peeked out the window and shook her head. "Every single morning," she sighed, but she was smiling.

lt:L1.01:3.text: Outside, the truck coughed, sputtered, and finally started with a satisfying roar. Sam waved at the neighbor, who waved back, covered in oil and grinning proudly.

t2:L1.01:0.text: sputtered. Sputtered means made short, uneven, coughing sounds (like an engine that won't start smoothly).

q:L1.01:0.text: What was the loud noise, really?

q:L1.01:1.text: How do you think the mother really felt about the noise — annoyed, amused, both? Why do you think that?

lt:L1.02:0.text: Sam felt nervous walking into the new classroom. Everyone else already seemed to know each other, chatting and laughing near the window.

lt:L1.02:1.text: Sam picked a desk near the back and sat down quietly, hoping nobody would notice how fast their heart was beating. Then a girl named Mia turned around and smiled.

lt:L1.02:2.text: "Are you new? I sat exactly where you are on my first day too," she said.

lt:L1.02:3.text: "It gets easier by lunchtime, I promise." Sam felt a small knot of worry loosen. Maybe today wouldn't be so bad after all.

t2:L1.02:0.text: nervous. Nervous means feeling worried or a little scared about something that's about to happen.

q:L1.02:0.text: How did Sam feel at the very start of the story? How do you know?

q:L1.02:1.text: Why do you think Mia's words helped Sam feel better?

lt:L1.03:0.text: At the big race, cars zoom around the track faster than the eye can follow. But every few laps, a driver has to pull into a special lane called the pit.

lt:L1.03:1.text: There, a whole team is waiting — not to rest, but to work at incredible speed. In under ten seconds, they can change all four tires, clean the windshield, and send the car roaring back onto the track.

lt:L1.03:2.text: Everyone has one exact job, and they practice it over and over so nothing goes wrong when it really counts. A single second lost in the pit can cost a driver the whole race.

t2:L1.03:0.text: incredible. Incredible means so surprising or impressive that it's hard to believe.

q:L1.03:0.text: Why does the team practice their jobs "over and over," according to the passage?

q:L1.03:1.text: What do you think would happen if the pit crew were slow?

lt:L1.04:0.text: Every Tuesday, a truck brings fresh bread to Mr. Iqbal's small shop before sunrise.

lt:L1.04:1.text: He counts on it — his whole morning depends on those loaves being on the shelf before the first customers arrive. But this Tuesday, seven o'clock came and went, and the truck never appeared.

lt:L1.04:2.text: Mr. Iqbal called the bakery three times, growing more frustrated with each unanswered ring.

lt:L1.04:3.text: Finally, his daughter suggested checking the neighborhood group chat — and there it was: the delivery driver's van had a flat tire two streets away. Mr.

lt:L1.04:4.text: Iqbal grabbed his bicycle pump without a second thought and pedaled over to help.

t2:L1.04:0.text: frustrated. Frustrated means annoyed and a little helpless because something isn't working the way you need it to.

q:L1.04:0.text: What problem did Mr. Iqbal have, and how did he find out what caused it?

q:L1.04:1.text: What does it tell you about Mr. Iqbal that he grabbed his bicycle pump to go help?

read:L1.05:B:5.text: Dan and Pam got a tip.

lt:L1.05:title.text: A Dog for the Whole Street.

lt:L1.05:0.text: When old Mrs. Chaudhry got too tired to walk her dog Bruno every morning, the neighbors worried he'd be stuck inside all day.

lt:L1.05:1.text: Instead, something wonderful happened: a rotation started. On Mondays, the twins next door took Bruno to the park.

lt:L1.05:2.text: On Tuesdays, it was the teenager from the corner house, who said walking Bruno was the only exercise he actually enjoyed. By the weekend, half the street had a turn.

lt:L1.05:3.text: Bruno, delighted, seemed to know exactly whose door to wait outside each morning, tail thumping the second the right person stepped out.

t2:L1.05:0.text: rotation. Rotation means a system where people take turns doing something, one after another in order.

q:L1.05:0.text: What problem did the street solve, and how?

q:L1.05:1.text: How did Bruno seem to feel about the new arrangement — what in the story tells you that?

read:L1.06:A:1.text: The cat sat on a mat.

read:L1.06:A:2.text: Sam said, "Is the cat sick?" The cat is not sick.

read:L1.06:B:2.text: Dan said, "Is a sack on top?" The sack is not on top.

lt:L1.06:0.text: In everyday English, if someone says a person "got the sack," they don't mean an actual bag — they mean the person lost their job. Nobody agrees exactly where the phrase came from, but one popular idea goes back hundreds of years, when tradesmen carried their own tools to work in a sack.

lt:L1.06:1.text: If you were let go, you packed up your sack of tools and left — hence "getting the sack." Whether or not that story is completely accurate, the phrase has stuck around for so long that most English speakers use it without ever thinking about actual sacks at all.

t2:L1.06:0.text: expression. Expression means a phrase people commonly use that means something different from its exact words.

q:L1.06:0.text: What does "getting the sack" actually mean?

q:L1.06:1.text: Why does the passage say we might use an expression "without ever thinking about" what it originally meant?

read:L1.07:A:3.text: The nut is in the cup.

read:L1.07:A:4.text: Is the nut in the cup?

read:L1.07:A:5.text: The nut is in the cup.

read:L1.07:B:5.text: Dan is not at the dock.

lt:L1.07:0.text: On busy construction sites, supervisors learned something surprising: workers who took one proper ten-minute break mid-morning, every single day at the same time, made fewer mistakes in the afternoon than workers who pushed through without stopping. It seemed backwards at first — how could stopping work make people more productive?

lt:L1.07:1.text: But the body and brain both need small pauses to reset concentration, especially doing careful, repetitive tasks in the heat. Now some companies build the "ten o'clock rule" right into the schedule: everyone stops together, drinks water, and stretches — no exceptions, not even for the boss.

t2:L1.07:0.text: productive. Productive means getting a lot of useful work done, not just being busy.

q:L1.07:0.text: What did supervisors notice about workers who took a proper break?

q:L1.07:1.text: Why do you think the passage says "no exceptions, not even for the boss"?

lt:L1.08:0.text: Before smartphones and ride-share apps existed, neighbors organized a shared morning school run with nothing more than a notebook taped inside someone's kitchen cabinet. Every family wrote down which mornings they could take the children, and everyone else simply trusted the schedule.

lt:L1.08:1.text: It sounds old-fashioned, but the system worked because everyone had something to lose if they broke the trust — miss your turn, and you'd better believe your neighbors would remember. These days, apps handle the scheduling, but the core idea hasn't changed at all: a group of people agreeing to share both the effort and the waiting, so no single person carries the whole burden alone.

t2:L1.08:0.text: schedule. Schedule means a plan that says when things will happen, especially times and dates.

q:L1.08:0.text: How did the old-fashioned rotation keep people honest, without any app?

q:L1.08:1.text: What is the "core idea" the passage says hasn't changed, even with new technology?

read:L1.09:A:0.text: Let me get the big bug!

read:L1.09:A:1.text: The bug is on the bed.

read:L1.09:B:0.text: Let me get the big bag.

read:L1.09:B:1.text: The bag is at the dock.

read:L1.09:B:4.text: Dan let Nat get the bag.

lt:L1.09:0.text: When a stranger's bag turns up with no name on it, most people feel a small pull in two directions at once — curiosity about what's inside, and a clear sense that opening it isn't quite right. Workplaces that handle a lot of lost property usually have a simple rule for this: log it, store it somewhere safe, and hold it for a set number of days before deciding what happens next.

lt:L1.09:1.text: It sounds almost too basic to matter, but that small bit of structure is exactly what stops an honest mistake from turning into an argument later about who touched what, and when.

t2:L1.09:0.text: curiosity. Curiosity means a strong wish to know or learn something.

q:L1.09:0.text: What two feelings does the passage say people get when they find an unlabeled bag?

q:L1.09:1.text: Why does having a simple rule (log it, store it, wait) help avoid arguments later?

read:L1.10:A:2.text: The doll sits on the bed.

read:L1.10:B:3.text: Nat tells Dan, "The bag is full."

lt:L1.10:0.text: English is full of words that look and sound exactly the same but mean completely different things depending on how they're used — linguists call these homonyms. "Well" can mean a deep hole dug for water, or it can mean feeling healthy, or it can mean "okay, so..." at the start of a sentence.

lt:L1.10:1.text: "Bill" can be a person's name, a piece of paper telling you what you owe, or the beak of a bird. Context — the words around a word — is what tells a listener or reader which meaning is meant.

lt:L1.10:2.text: This is exactly why understanding a whole sentence matters so much more than knowing single words in isolation.

t2:L1.10:0.text: context. Context means the words, situation, or information around something that helps explain what it means.

q:L1.10:0.text: What are two completely different meanings of the word "bill," according to the passage?

q:L1.10:1.text: Why does the passage say context matters more than knowing single words alone?

read:L1.11:B:5.text: They get a van at the dock.

lt:L1.11:0.text: The word "vet" hides a small trap: most people think first of an animal doctor, but "vet" is also short for "veteran" — someone who has served in the military — and it's a verb too, as in "the company vetted every new driver before hiring them," meaning they checked the person's background carefully. Three different meanings, one small word, and only the sentence around it tells you which one is meant.

lt:L1.11:1.text: Careful readers learn to slow down for a half-second whenever a short, familiar-looking word suddenly doesn't quite fit the sentence — that pause is often the first sign a word is doing a job you didn't expect.

t2:L1.11:0.text: veteran. Veteran means someone with a lot of experience, especially someone who has served in the armed forces.

q:L1.11:0.text: Name the three different meanings of "vet" the passage describes.

q:L1.11:1.text: What does the passage suggest a careful reader should do when a short word "doesn't quite fit"?

read:L1.12:A:2.text: The fox naps in the box.

read:L1.12:B:2.text: Dan and Nat fix a van.

lt:L1.12:0.text: Every single letter of the English alphabet has now had its own proper introduction — some of them, like c and k, even share a job. It took twelve lessons to get here, on purpose: rushing through all 26 letters in a week or two sounds efficient, but it means most of them never get practiced enough to become automatic.

lt:L1.12:1.text: From here, nothing new needs to be "discovered" — the next lessons are about combining these same 26 letters in cleverer and cleverer ways: two letters making one sound, sounds joining into longer words, and patterns repeating across hundreds of different words once you know what to look for.

t2:L1.12:0.text: automatic. Automatic means happening without needing to think about it carefully each time, because it's been practiced so much.

q:L1.12:0.text: Why does the passage say rushing through all 26 letters quickly would actually be worse, not better?

q:L1.12:1.text: What does the passage say comes next, now that all 26 letters are taught?

read:L1.13:A:2.text: The dog and the pig run.

read:L1.13:B:2.text: The tag said "b." Dan said, "d?" No, it was "b." It was a big mess at the dock.

lt:L1.13:0.text: In busy warehouses, a single misread letter on a shipping label can send a package hundreds of miles in the wrong direction. That's why professional warehouse workers are trained to read labels a specific, careful way: never glance quickly at a whole word and guess, but check the exact letters, especially any that could be confused with another — b and d, or the number 0 and the letter O.

lt:L1.13:1.text: Some warehouses even print certain confusable letters in a special typeface designed to make them look as different from each other as possible. It's a small design choice built entirely around a very human, very ordinary reading mistake.

t2:L1.13:0.text: typeface. Typeface means a particular style or design of printed letters.

q:L1.13:0.text: Why does the passage say warehouse workers are trained not to "glance quickly and guess" at labels?

q:L1.13:1.text: What did some warehouses design specifically to solve the b/d mix-up problem?

lt:L1.14:0.text: Fourteen lessons ago, this course started with three sounds and a handful of made-up "alien words." Today's check uses every single letter in English, a spelling rule, a plural ending, and twenty-four words that don't even follow the normal rules — and asks for all of it back, cold, without any warm-up hints. That's not a small ask.

lt:L1.14:1.text: Whatever the score turns out to be, getting through fourteen full lessons of new material, in order, each one building on the last, is real, durable progress — the kind that doesn't disappear the way a memorized page would. What comes next, in Level 2, isn't starting over; it's the exact same skill, aimed at bigger and bigger words.

t2:L1.14:0.text: durable. Durable means lasting a long time without wearing out or disappearing.

q:L1.14:0.text: What does the passage say is different about a "durable" skill compared to a memorized page?

q:L1.14:1.text: How does the passage describe what Level 2 will be, compared to Level 1?
